contentHtml:
A receipt service passes GET /health, yet a customer gets an error when creating a receipt. Trace the failed POST to the service's Linux identity, locate the missing permission, then repeat the operation with a fresh name.

Start the lab

Use Bash and Docker on a disposable Linux host. From the repository root, start an isolated container and copy in the receipt service. The HTTP client and server both run on the container's loopback interface. All files and numeric identities used below belong to this lab.

lab=$(docker run --rm -d --network none python:3.13-slim-bookworm sleep infinity)
docker cp examples/operational-scenarios/runtime-and-platform/service-write-permission/receipt-service.py "$lab:/tmp/receipt-service.py"
docker exec -it "$lab" bash

Run the following commands inside that same container shell until cleanup. The shell has authority to prepare the fixture and change its permissions. The directory owner (UID 20001) and the service (UID 10001, GID 10001) are distinct. Record the original numeric owners, groups and modes before starting the service.

umask 077
labdir=/srv/receipt-lab
outbox=$labdir/outbox
install -d -o 20001 -g 10001 -m 0710 "$labdir"
install -d -o 20001 -g 10001 -m 0770 "$outbox"
chmod 0444 /tmp/receipt-service.py
record_modes() { stat -c '%n %u:%g %a' "$labdir" "$outbox"; }
record_modes | tee /tmp/receipt-modes.before

setpriv --reuid=10001 --regid=10001 --clear-groups --no-new-privs \
  python /tmp/receipt-service.py "$outbox" >/tmp/receipt-service.log 2>&1 &
service_pid=$!

Expect 20001:10001 710 for the parent and 20001:10001 770 for the outbox. The service group can traverse the parent and create files in the outbox. Other users have no access to either directory.

Establish the user-visible baseline

Define a small client that prints both status and response body. Use it for all three receipt requests. Each name is synthetic and may be created once.

request() {
  python - "$@" <<'PY'
import sys
from http.client import HTTPConnection

method, path = sys.argv[1:]
client = HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 18083, timeout=3)
client.request(method, path)
response = client.getresponse()
print(f"HTTP {response.status} {response.read().decode().strip()}")
client.close()
PY
}
wait_ready() {
  local attempt
  for attempt in {1..30}; do
    if [[ "$(request GET /health 2>/dev/null)" == 'HTTP 200 ready' ]]; then
      echo 'HTTP 200 ready'
      return 0
    fi
    sleep 0.1
  done
  echo 'Readiness check timed out' >&2
  cat /tmp/receipt-service.log >&2
  return 1
}

Gate the first write on the health response. If startup times out, inspect the service log before proceeding.

wait_ready &&
  request POST /receipts/baseline.txt &&
  stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$outbox/baseline.txt" &&
  cat "$outbox/baseline.txt"

Before changing permissions, confirm HTTP 201 created baseline.txt and a file owned by 10001:10001 with mode 600 and content receipt baseline.txt.

Reproduce the failure and identify the missing permission

As the lab operator, remove the group write bit on the outbox. Send the same kind of request with a new name. Read the service log for this specific request and path, and check whether a file appeared.

chmod g-w "$outbox"
request POST /receipts/denied.txt
request GET /health
grep -F "POST /receipts/denied.txt path=$outbox/denied.txt" /tmp/receipt-service.log
test ! -e "$outbox/denied.txt" && echo 'denied.txt is absent'

Expect HTTP 500 write failed, HTTP 200 ready and no new file. The matching log line identifies the path the service tried to create.

POST /receipts/denied.txt path=/srv/receipt-lab/outbox/denied.txt error=Permission denied

Collect the following evidence before repairing the directory.

grep -E '^(Name|State|Uid|Gid|Groups|CapEff):' "/proc/$service_pid/status"
namei -l "$outbox"
record_modes
setpriv --reuid=20001 --regid=20001 --clear-groups test -w "$outbox" &&
  echo 'The directory owner still has write access'
  • The original PID still exists. The second and fourth entries of Uid and Gid are the effective and filesystem IDs. Both are 10001 here. Groups is empty (no supplementary groups), and CapEff is zero.
  • namei -l shows search permission (x) on each directory in the path. / and /srv allow traversal, and group 10001 has x on receipt-lab and outbox.
  • The outbox is still 20001:10001, now mode 750. UID 20001 can still write as its owner. The service matches the group, whose permissions are now r-x. Creating the new entry requires both w and x on that directory. The missing bit is g+w on the outbox.

Restore access and prove recovery

Restore that one bit, compare the directory metadata with the baseline, then submit a fresh receipt through the running service.

chmod g+w "$outbox"
record_modes | diff -u /tmp/receipt-modes.before -
request POST /receipts/recovered.txt
stat -c '%u:%g %a %n' "$outbox/recovered.txt"
cat "$outbox/recovered.txt"
grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|Groups|CapEff):' "/proc/$service_pid/status"

An empty diff confirms the original owners, groups and modes. Expect HTTP 201 created recovered.txt and a new file containing receipt recovered.txt, owned by 10001:10001 with mode 600. The same service PID still has its original credentials. This correction gives the service group the required write access and keeps other users excluded.

If the actual path, credentials or mode differ, preserve the request, log and process evidence for the storage owner. Check mount options, ACLs or security policy before changing any further permissions. See Storage, Backup and Recovery and the container troubleshooting runbook.

Clean up

Run exit to leave the container shell. In the original host shell, stop the lab container. Docker removes the container and its synthetic files because it was started with --rm.

docker stop "$lab"

The Linux manuals describe credential fields, directory search permission, and file creation failures. proc_pid_status(5), path_resolution(7) and open(2).
